passages.t: A sad face before the king
passages.happening:
‘Now in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was set before him, I took the wine and gave it to the king’ (verse 1). Nehemiah had never been sad in the king's presence, and the king notices: “Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart” (verse 2). ‘I was overwhelmed with fear’ (verse 2).

Nehemiah answers, “May the king live forever! Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?” (verse 3).

“What is your request?” replied the king (verse 4). ‘So I prayed to the God of heaven’ (verse 4), and then Nehemiah asks to be sent to Judah, ‘to the city where my fathers are buried, so that I may rebuild it’ (verse 5).

The king, with the queen sitting beside him, asks how long he will be gone, and Nehemiah sets a time (verse 6). He asks for letters to the governors west of the Euphrates for safe passage, and a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest, for timber for the gates, the city wall and his own house. ‘And because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Nisan, in March and April, of Artaxerxes' twentieth year was the spring of 445 BC, about four months after the news came.

At the Persian court, sorrow in the king's presence could be dangerous. The king's company was supposed to be a place of joy, and a gloomy servant might be suspected of discontent or of plotting. That is why Nehemiah was afraid.

There was more to fear. The king himself had earlier ordered the work on Jerusalem's walls stopped until he gave further orders (Ezra 4:21). Nehemiah was asking him to reverse his own decision. So he answers shrewdly. He speaks first of the place where his fathers are buried, appealing to the duty every people felt to honor its ancestors' graves, and he does not name Jerusalem, a city the king had reason to suspect.

Between the king's question and his answer, he prays to the God of heaven. After months of prayer, a quick silent prayer in the moment is enough.

The letters he asks for were the ordinary papers of Persian travel and government. The word for the king's forest, pardes, is a Persian word for an enclosed park. Its Greek form later gave English its word paradise.
passages.later:
Ezra had used the same words for God's guidance a few years before: ‘for the gracious hand of his God was upon him’ (Ezra 7:9).

And the order Nehemiah asked the king to undo is in Ezra: ‘issue an order for these men to stop, so that this city will not be rebuilt until I so order’ (Ezra 4:21).
passages.asks: Nehemiah prayed for months, then prayed again in a single breath, and then asked boldly. Ask what you need to bring to God before you bring it to the person who can help. And ask whether you are as careful with your words as you are sincere in your prayers.

passages.t: The road to Judah, and a ride by night
passages.happening:
‘Then I went to the governors west of the Euphrates and gave them the king’s letters. The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me’ (verse 9).

Two men hear of it and are not pleased. ‘But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard about this, they were deeply disturbed that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites’ (verse 10).

Three days after he reaches Jerusalem, Nehemiah gets up at night with a few men. ‘I did not tell anyone what my God had laid on my heart to do for Jerusalem’ (verse 12). He goes out through the Valley Gate and inspects the broken walls and burned gates. At the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, ‘there was no room for the animal under me to get through’ (verse 14), so he goes up the valley by night and looks at the wall, and then he comes back. The officials do not know where he has been (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The escort of officers and cavalry fits the standing of a royal appointee. Later the book shows that Nehemiah had been made governor of Judah (5:14).

His opponents were significant men. Sanballat is named in letters of about 407 BC from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt as governor of Samaria, the province to the north. Horonite probably links him with Beth-horon, a town northwest of Jerusalem, or with Horonaim in Moab. Tobiah, called the Ammonite official, probably held authority in the lands east of the Jordan; a family known as the Tobiads was powerful there in later centuries, and many scholars connect him with it. A rebuilt Jerusalem threatened the influence they held over Judah.

The night ride shows prudence. Nehemiah tells no one his plans until he has seen the damage for himself. He rides out on the west, goes south, and turns up the eastern side of the city, where rubble blocks his animal. Excavations on the eastern slope of the City of David, among them Kathleen Kenyon's in the 1960s, found collapsed stone terraces there, which fits a slope choked with debris.
passages.later: Nehemiah traveled with soldiers where Ezra had refused them: Ezra ‘was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road’ (Ezra 8:22).
passages.asks: Nehemiah looked at the ruins for himself, by night, before he said a word. Ask whether you take time to see a problem clearly before you speak about it. And ask what God has laid on your heart that you have not yet told anyone.

passages.happening:
Then Nehemiah calls the people. “You see the trouble we are in. Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned down. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace” (verse 17). He tells them about the gracious hand of his God on him and what the king had said. “Let us start rebuilding,” they replied, ‘and they set their hands to this good work’ (verse 18).

But Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem the Arab mock them: “What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?” (verse 19).

Nehemiah answers, “The God of heaven is the One who will grant us success. We, His servants, will start rebuilding, but you have no portion, right, or claim in Jerusalem” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Disgrace, cherpah, is the key word of Nehemiah's call. In the ancient world a ruined city shamed its people, and for Israel it shamed the God whose name was attached to Jerusalem. Rebuilding was a matter of honor, God's more than theirs.

The verb in ‘they set their hands to this good work’ (verse 18) is chazaq, to be strong. They took courage and set to it. The same verb will come again and again in chapter 3 as the word for repairing the wall, so the strengthening of the people and of the wall go together.

The third opponent, Geshem the Arab, probably stood for the Arab kingdom of Qedar to the south, which controlled trade routes. A silver bowl found at Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt names a Qaynu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar, whom many identify as Geshem's son.

The charge of rebellion was dangerous, because the king had stopped the earlier rebuilding on just such grounds. Nehemiah's reply uses the language of law and inheritance: no portion, no right, no claim. He denies his opponents any standing in the city of God.
passages.later: The opponents' charge was the one that had worked before, when officials told the king that Jerusalem was ‘a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces’ (Ezra 4:15).
passages.asks: Nehemiah told the people what God had done and invited them in, and they agreed to start. Ask whether you invite others into good work, or try to do it alone. And ask how you answer mockery: with anger, or with the quiet confidence of verse 20.
